vignette: Mr. Thompson is a 71-year-old security guard who has been married for over four decades. On September 11, 2001, he was working at one of the buildings near the World Trade Center when the attack occurred. The traumatic event left him with vivid and detailed memories that continue to haunt his daily life. Since the attack, Mr. Thompson has found it almost impossible to cope with any form of distress or upset. He often ruminates on how he might have prevented what happened, and this self-comparison with others who may not have gotten into a similar situation exacerbates his feelings of inadequacy. His negative appraisals about himself as someone unable to manage stress lead him to adopt maladaptive strategies that offer temporary relief but ultimately reinforce his distress. One of these strategies is always sitting with his back against a wall so he can see the room and monitor potential threats, which helps mitigate some of his hypervigilance. However, this behavior has also made it increasingly difficult for him to socialize or feel comfortable in public spaces, further isolating him from others. Mr. Thompson's tendency to ruminate about revenge against those responsible for the attack has only deepened his sense of failure and frustration. The clarity of his memories is particularly troubling; they are so vivid that he can relive every detail as if it were happening all over again. This recurrent reliving often leads him to feel numb and detached, as if the events happened to someone else. He struggles to piece together a coherent narrative of what occurred on that day, which further compounds his feelings of helplessness. His hypervigilance extends into his interactions with people, making it difficult for him to trust even those he knows well. This constant state of alertness makes it hard for him to engage in conversations without feeling anxious and suspicious. As a result, Mr. Thompson's relationships at work have become strained; colleagues find his behavior unpredictable and sometimes confrontational. Mr. Thompson’s wife has noticed these changes over time and worries about the impact on their relationship. His rigid need to always be alert has made it difficult for them to enjoy social activities together, leading to increased tension and isolation. He is now at a point where he recognizes that these behaviors are affecting his life in profound ways. What finally brought Mr. Thompson to seek help was a recent incident at work where his hypervigilance led him to overreact to a situation, causing a minor disturbance among the other staff members. The cumulative effect of his maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals had become too overwhelming to ignore. He is most afraid that he will lose control again and further damage his relationships with his wife and colleagues. However, he also harbors a glimmer of hope that therapy can help him manage these thoughts and behaviors more effectively, allowing him to regain some sense of normalcy in his life.
